technical_gaps.description: sdk-retry (caller check 1): what microsoft-graph-core 2.0.4's RetryHandler does by default. VERIFICATION LIMIT: the sources jar is present (~/.m2/repository/com/microsoft/graph/microsoft-graph-core/2.0.4/microsoft-graph-core-2.0.4-sources.jar). Grep against its uncompressed central directory confirmed it contains com/microsoft/graph/httpcore/RetryHandler.java, httpcore/middlewareoption/RetryOptions.java, httpcore/HttpClients.java, http/CoreHttpProvider.java and http/GraphServiceException.java. The entry BODIES are deflate-compressed, and this stage has no unzip/bash tool, so their source could not be read. The following comes from the upstream msgraph-sdk-java-core 2.0.x source and is unverified against the local jar. GraphServiceClient.builder().authenticationProvider(p).buildClient() uses HttpClients.createDefault(p), which installs AuthenticationHandler, RetryHandler (default RetryOptions), RedirectHandler and TelemetryHandler. RetryOptions defaults: maxRetries 3, delay 3 s (hard caps MAX_RETRIES 10, MAX_DELAY 180 s). It retries ONLY 429, 503 and 504, and only when the request body is buffered (known Content-Length, which is true for the sendMail JSON POST). The wait honours a Retry-After header parsed as integer seconds; without one it uses exponential backoff with jitter. Each wait is capped at 180 s and is a Thread.sleep on the calling (Tomcat) thread. After exhaustion, the final 429/503/504 response reaches CoreHttpProvider, which throws GraphServiceException (GraphFatalServiceException for 5xx) with getResponseCode() set. Consequences: (a) a throttled request can hold a request thread for up to about 3 x 180 s in the worst case; (b) 503/504 retries of a non-idempotent sendMail POST can deliver a duplicate email if Graph had in fact accepted the first attempt; (c) an HTTP-date Retry-After would fail parseLong and surface as an unexpected error (MGE-B-004/500).
technical_gaps.recommendation_or_open_question: 03_implement Step 0 must confirm this with unzip before writing the E15-E17 tests. Keep the defaults per the user's Q4=A. If (a) or (b) matters operationally, a custom RetryOptions (fewer retries, no 503/504) is a follow-up, not this feature.

technical_gaps.description: retry-after (caller check 2): whether Retry-After can be read from the GraphServiceException thrown after retries run out. UNVERIFIED for the same reason (compressed jar). Upstream 2.0.x GraphServiceException.createFromResponse copies every response header into a private List<String> responseHeaders, formatted 'Name : value'. Whether 2.0.4 exposes it through a public getter (getResponseHeaders()) could not be confirmed. getResponseCode() == 429 is reliably available either way, so the 429 status mapping itself is not at risk.
technical_gaps.recommendation_or_open_question: If a getter exists, parse the first entry whose name (before ' : ') equalsIgnoreCase 'Retry-After' and pass the value through as MGE-B-002's retryAfter (E15). If none exists, return 429 without the header (E16 behaviour for every 429) and amend the E15 acceptance criterion. Do NOT add an OkHttp interceptor or a reflection hack to recover it (scope).

technical_gaps.description: graph exception message leak: upstream GraphServiceException.getMessage() (non-verbose) includes the HTTP method, the request URL (/users/{from}/sendMail) and the first ~50 characters of the request body, which typically include the subject and recipients. technical_gaps.description: The BOM parent is 4.1.0 (Spring Boot 4), and the wealth handler imports tools.jackson.core.JacksonException. So Spring MVC binds JSON with Jackson 3, and the pom's pinned com.fasterxml jackson-databind 2.17.1 plays no part in request binding. @JsonAlias stays in com.fasterxml.jackson.annotation, which Jackson 3 still honours.

technical_gaps.description: Validation single path (divergence from the spec). The spec keeps the generated Bean Validation (MVC @Valid), calls jakarta Validator again in the service, and maps violations through a shared mapper. That design is internally inconsistent. MVC rejects bean violations (V-001 null, V-003, V-004, V-005) before the service's custom checks run (V-002 regex, blank, V-008, V-007), and MethodArgumentNotValidException reports a Set of violations. So the same request can get V-003 over HTTP but V-002 in-process, which breaks spec 3.6's 'same code either way' and its 3.5 ordering. Setting useBeanValidation=false makes EmailServiceImpl the only validator for both paths. It is deterministic, needs no Validator injection, no violation mapper, and no MethodArgumentNotValid/ConstraintViolation handlers. It is also how the current EmailServiceImpl already works.
technical_gaps.recommendation_or_open_question: Adopted. Contract maxLength/maxItems stay as documentation of the defaults. If the user insists on the spec's design, the fix for the ordering problem is for the handler to re-run the service validator on MethodArgumentNotValidException.getBindingResult().getTarget().

technical_gaps.description: In-process contract change versus spec 3.6. The exceptions expose getCode() (and getRetryAfter()) but NOT getStatus(), per exception-handling.md's pitfall 'Don't put HTTP status logic inside the exception class'. EmailValidationException is reused unchanged (it already has (code, message)). EmailConfigurationException stays as a distinct typed exception for misconfiguration.
technical_gaps.recommendation_or_open_question: Features 2 and 4 map on exception type plus code. That is enough for EML009/EML010 mapping. Record this in feature 2's spec.

technical_gaps.description: The spec asks for MockMvc/WebMvc tests, including 'without a JWT gets 401 and never reaches EmailService'. testing-patterns.md forbids @WebMvcTest/MockMvc by default. A @SpringBootTest would also need the AZURE_* placeholders (GraphProperties is always bound) and any other starter prerequisites, and no context test exists in this service today. So the 401 path is not exercised by a test. Coverage instead comes from: the reflection check of @JwtSecured, the AccessDeniedException-to-403 handler test, and the grep in Step 10 proving the path left permit-all-urls. The 401 itself is the starter's unchanged anyRequest().authenticated() behaviour.

technical_gaps.description: This is a breaking HTTP change (accepted, Q2=A). The envelope changes, `name` becomes `fileName` (the alias is kept), and a JWT with ROLE_APP_NOTIFICATION is now required. Operational follow-up: the token issuer must grant APP_NOTIFICATION to calling applications before deploy. Ordering nuance: a malformed body is rejected with 400 (V-006) during argument binding, before the @JwtSecured aspect runs, so a valid-JWT caller without the role and sending bad JSON gets 400, not 403. Unauthenticated callers still get 401 first.
technical_gaps.recommendation_or_open_question: Announce the change to consumers. The ordering nuance is acceptable.

plan_critique.acceptance_criteria_coverage: partial. Every behavioural criterion (envelope, multi-recipient, TEXT/HTML, saveToSentItems, E3-E8, E10-E12, aliases, 401 retry, 429 + Retry-After, 502/500 mapping, in-process V-003/V-007, log hygiene, apiCollection, the token-log removal, permit-all removal, @JwtSecured, allowed-senders and max-total config) has a target file and a test. Five criteria are deliberately AMENDED and need user sign-off: (1) 'none define max-subject-length, max-body-length or max-attachments' is replaced by 'these 3 keys are kept; only max-attachment-size-bytes is removed'; (2) 'EmailConfigurationException is deleted' is replaced by 'kept, mapped to 500 by the catch-all'; (3) 'MockMvc/WebMvc tests' are replaced by direct-construction tests, and the 'no JWT gets 401' test is not written (see technical_gaps); (4) E15's Retry-After header is conditional on the SDK exposing response headers; (5) spec 3.6's getStatus() becomes getCode(). The E11 request-size cap is covered, by an interceptor rather than a filter.
blast_radius_concerns: openapi.yaml: removing EmailSendResponse/ErrorResponse and renaming name to fileName breaks every existing HTTP caller (accepted, Q2=A). No other schema references them (grep-verified).
GlobalExceptionHandler's basePackages also covers ApplicationController (/api/v1/info). Its unexpected errors now come back as a GenericResponse 500 instead of EmailSendResponse. That is harmless.
Removing /api/v1/email/send from permit-all in all 6 profiles means every environment needs callers holding APP_NOTIFICATION tokens at deploy time.
The EmailService signature change (to void) has no callers besides EmailController today (grep-verified). Features 2 and 4 will build on the new signature.

scope_expansion_critique.delete_config_keys: Rejected in part. Deleting max-attachment-size-bytes is a direct consequence of the user's Q5=A: it is replaced by max-total-attachment-size-bytes, and the per-file cap was the rejected option C. It is therefore in scope. Deleting max-subject-length, max-body-length and max-attachments was the spec's own idea. Its 'one source of truth' argument only holds if generated Bean Validation enforces the limits, and that design breaks the spec's own deterministic ordering and HTTP/in-process parity (technical_gaps 'validation single path'). Keeping the keys means no yml churn for them, the existing EmailProperties fields stay, and the service keeps enforcing them as it does today. The remaining risk is that the contract's documented maxLength drifts if someone overrides a key. That is low and cosmetic.
scope_expansion_critique.delete_EmailConfigurationException: Rejected. It was not requested, and it gives a smaller diff only on paper (the throw site changes, a file is deleted, and the in-process contract changes). A missing Graph client is a distinct failure mode: misconfiguration, not a Graph failure. exception-handling.md asks for one typed exception per distinct failure mode. The rewritten handler's catch-all already returns 500 and logs MGE-B-004 for it, which satisfies spec E19 with zero new code. The class is left untouched.
scope_expansion_critique.content_length_filter_vs_spring_settings: A cap is needed: the user chose 'servlet cap' in Q5=A, and the 512m heap would otherwise buffer an arbitrarily large JSON body before the decoded-total check. The spec is right that Spring's settings do not cover it. server.tomcat.max-http-form-post-size applies only to application/x-www-form-urlencoded parameter parsing. spring.servlet.multipart.max-file-size/max-request-size apply only to multipart/form-data. server.tomcat.max-swallow-size only limits how many bytes Tomcat discards after an aborted upload; it never rejects an accepted body. Spring Boot exposes no Tomcat property that caps a JSON request body. The spec's OncePerRequestFilter is still heavier than needed: it would hand-serialise a second copy of the envelope (ObjectMapper and correlation logic), and its order relative to the security chain needs care (a 413 could precede the 401 for unauthenticated callers). A HandlerInterceptor scoped to /api/v1/email/send runs before @RequestBody is read, runs after security, and throws EmailValidationException(MGE-V-008), which the one GlobalExceptionHandler renders. It is the same derived limit with less code and a single envelope source.
